data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"As n grows, the probability of reaching unanimous consensus tends to 0. Majority dynamics here is monotone local search for MaxCut: a vertex with two or more opposite-color neighbors flips, strictly decreasing the number of crossing edges; a vertex with two or more same-color neighbors never flips. Hence the cut size is non-increasing and the process is absorbed in finite time into a locally stable configuration where every vertex has at least two same-color neighbors, i.e., crossing edges form a matching. Since a uniformly random start has ~1.5n crossing edges while a locally optimal mixed cut on a random cubic graph has \u0398(n) crossing edges concentrated around a constant fraction of n, the process almost never reaches the cut of size 0 (consensus); it halts in a mixed locally stable state whp.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the asynchronous random update order could increase cut size (it cannot: only unstable vertices flip, each flip strictly reduces cut size), the monotonicity argument fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If locally optimal cuts reachable from a random start overwhelmingly included the empty cut with probability bounded away from 0, consensus probability would instead be a positive constant.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the final-cut fraction on random 3-regular graphs concentrated at 0 (all local optima were near-consensus), the whp-nonconsensus conclusion would fail.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Cut-size monotonicity: each update replaces a vertex's color only when it disagrees with a strict majority of neighbors, which removes 2 or 3 crossing edges and adds 0 or 1, so the number of crossing edges strictly decreases at every update. The process therefore terminates in at most ~1.5n updates at a configuration where every vertex has crossing-degree 0 (consensus) or 1 (a matching of crossing edges). On random 3-regular graphs, which are sparse expanders but locally tree-like, local search for MaxCut is known empirically and semi-rigorously to stall at cuts well below the global maximum and far above zero: the final cut is a nonzero matching-cut with \u0398(n) edges. Consensus is reached only if this matching is empty, an event with probability o(1) as n grows.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
